newsitem.title: USA: US senators seek veto-proof majority on nuke waste.
newsitem.headline: US senators seek veto-proof majority on nuke waste.

text.p: Senate supporters of a bill to store nuclear waste in Nevada were unsure Monday whether they would secure enough votes to override a threatened White House veto, Congressional and anti-nuclear officials said.
The Senate passed a similar bill last year by a vote of 63-37, four votes short of a veto-proof majority.
On Monday, Congressional and environmental officials said there could be anywhere from 31 to 38 votes against the bill, which is up for a final vote on Tuesday.
"It's very close to that (veto-proof) margin right now," said Bill Magavern, director of consumer group Public Citizen's anti-nuclear energy project.

Nuclear utilities, which have paid more than $8 billion into a U.S. nuclear waste fund, are pressing for a temporary storage facility for their spent fuel until the government has a permanent dump ready to bury their waste underground.
By law, the Energy Department was supposed to start taking responsibility for the waste by February 1998.
But the government does not expect to have a permanent dump ready until 2010 or 2015, assuming that Nevada's Yucca Mountain, the only site being investigated, proves to be safe for radioactive waste.
The bill by Sen. Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, would park the waste in Nevada near Yucca Mountain, whether or not the spent fuel was ultimately going to be buried in the mountain.
The waste could be stored somewhere else only in the unlikely event the president and Congress backed another site.

An amendment by Senator Jeff Bingaman, a New Mexico Democrat, would ensure that the waste would be sent to Nevada for temporary storage only if Yucca Mountain was definitely going to become the permanent dump.
"The only reason for putting the interim facility in Nevada is that that is where the permanent repository is going to be," Bingaman said on the Senate floor.
"We need to find another permanent repository if Yucca Mountain proves not to be ... right," he said.
Bingaman said he would vote against the whole bill if his amendment did not pass Tuesday.
Murkowski and the nuclear utilities oppose Bingaman's amendment because it would give the government a way out of building an interim storage site.

"If ... no site is chosen, we're right back to where we are. We're leaving (the spent fuel) where it is," said Murkowski, referring to the 80 sites in 41 states where nuclear utilities are storing their spent fuel in pools.
Energy Secretary Federico Pena said last week that despite changes approved so far which addressed some of the administration's concerns, the bill was still unacceptable.
